> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://docs.mcpjam.com/llms.txt
> Use

this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Evaluate

> Author test cases for your MCP server, run
them across models, and gate pass/fail on deterministic assertions plus optional LLM-as-judge.\n\nA benchmark score doesn't tell
you whether your server holds up in production. Evaluate lets you pin down the behaviors you care about (which tools fire, with wh

at arguments, what the final answer looks like) and run them across the models your users actually use.

## Requirements

Eval
s are available to both signed-in users and guests. Guests authenticate automatically using their guest session, so no sign-in is

required to run or generate tests.

## How it's organized

**1. Project**

Holds your servers and your suites. Everything be

low lives in one project.

**2. Suite**

A group of cases plus the defaults they share: attached servers, models to run agains

t, default assertions, judge config, and argument-matching mode.

**3. Case**

One scenario you want to verify: a prompt (or a
sequence of prompts), the tools you expect to fire, an optional expected output, and the assertions that decide pass/fail.\n\n**4
. Run**\n\nOne execution of a suite. Produces **iterations**: one per case × model. Each iteration has its own transcript, tool ca

lls, tokens, duration, and verdict.

## Authoring a case

Click **New case** in the suite header (or in the empty-state screen
when no cases exist yet) to open the case workspace. The case is a draft until you press **Save**: backing out without saving lea

ves your suite unchanged.

### Case workspace

The case editor is a two-pane workspace. The left column is where you write the
case; the right column shows the selected trial: a live run in progress, a persisted iteration from history, or a spec preview.\n

**Left column: the case spine**

Every case opens in the spine, however it was authored: in the app, through the CLI, or from
an SDK suite file. The spine is a flat, ordered list of steps. Each step is one of:\n\n* **Prompt**: a user turn the model receive
s. The first prompt is always present; use **Add assertion or action** to add a second prompt for multi-turn cases.\n* **Interact*

*: a widget interaction (click, typing) run against a live widget.
* **Assert**: an assertion that grades the case.

Below the

step list, an **Expected outcome** field holds the goal sentence the judge grades against.

**Assertions**

Use **Add assertio
n or action** to add an assertion, a second prompt, or an interact step. Each assertion row says what it checks, who wrote it, and
what a miss does:\n\n* **Route**: answers \"which tool should handle it?\" and carries that answer's strictness: *Reach the tool*
allows extra calls, *Exact route* requires the exact order with no extras. The route is always Required.\n* **Step N**: an assert
ion written as a step (what the CLI and the SDK produce). It is graded in place, at its position in the run, and is labelled by th
at position: a step-level \"no tool errors\" reads **No tool errors so far**, because it only sees the transcript up to that point
. Editing one rewrites that step; it never becomes a case-level assertion.\n* **This case**: an assertion you added here. It is gr
aded once, over the finished transcript.\n* **Suite**: a default the suite applies to every case. Read-only here, with a link to t
he suite's **Checks by stage** settings.\n\nThe list reads as a checklist with progressive disclosure. An off row shows only its s
hort name. Once on, clicking the name opens an inline editor showing the full criterion, the **Required / Advisory** role control,
and any editable fields (thresholds, match criteria). Multiple editors can stay open at once. An assertion that carries a number
(such as a latency budget) shows it under the name at rest.\n\nA row's **role** says what a miss does: **Required** fails the tria
l, **Advisory** shows the miss without failing it. The control appears when your deployment supports assertion policy; otherwise t
he role chip shows read-only with a tooltip explaining why it cannot be changed, for example, when the assertion is inherited from
the suite, or when the backend does not yet support assertion policy.\n\nBecause a failing required assertion halts the run, an a

ssertion written as a step can leave later assertions unrun. The trial column marks those **Skipped**.

**The route question**

The answer here is what marks a case negative: never an inference from its steps:

* **A named tool**: the case must take that
route.\n* **No tool should be called**: a negative case. It passes only if the model called nothing. An assertion that requires a
tool call contradicts this, and the spine says so.\n* **Any route**: the case names no route and is graded by its assertions. Thi
s is a normal positive case, and it is what most CLI- and SDK-authored cases are.\n\nA brand-new case that asserts nothing at all
